name: Karl Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on the tills at Fairmont Foods, the big store on the ring road, usually six till two. I scan, bag, sort out cards that fail, and when it's quiet I'm facing shelves or dragging cages out of the back. Half the day I'm also minding the self-checkouts, because they beep every thirty seconds. By two my feet are done and I go and get Josh and Ella from school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The regulars, honestly. Old Mr Dunne tells me about war films and the shift flies. What wears me out is the pay, the rota changing on a Thursday for the week ahead, and being told to smile while head office trims our hours. Four years in and I'm still on the bottom rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, fine, the machines were overhyped, but don't get comfortable. On the group chat with the other cashiers I'd probably post that nothing changes unless we push for it. Online I'd keep quiet, I'm not a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changing is not good news for me. My hours already got cut by six a week last spring and the mortgage deal runs out in two years. Plateau just means more of the same squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my shifts and go to the shopworkers' union meeting on the first Tuesday, which I've been skipping. I'd take any extra weekend shifts offered, even though Lena (my partner) hates me missing Sundays. And we'd stop the takeaway on Fridays, that's about forty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not fear, it's that dull weight of being one bill away from trouble. I look at the letterbox before I look at the kids some days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union meeting you've been skipping. What stops you going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's Tuesday evenings, the kids' homework, and a bit of feeling it won't change anything. But when the hours got cut, the people who got theirs back were the ones whose rep complained loudly. So I should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first if the hours dropped again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, and I'd ring them before they ring me. The mortgage never, the electric never. I've done the sums on a napkin: a six-hour cut means we're short about a hundred and eighty a month.

say: I'd tell colleagues the machines are **overhyped**, but that nobody should get comfortable.
I'd say in the group chat that things only improve if we **push** together.
think: Nothing changing means more of the **same squeeze** on my hours.
My shifts were cut by six a week and my **mortgage deal** ends in two years.
do: Keep working my shifts and take **extra weekend hours** if they offer them.
Go to the **union meeting** on the first Tuesday instead of skipping it.
Stop the Friday takeaway to save about **forty a week**.
feel: A dull **tiredness** from being one bill away from trouble.
S0.quote: Nothing changing is not good news for me. My hours already got cut by six a week last spring and the mortgage deal runs out in two years.
fieldNote: Karl treats an ordinary world as already **tight**, so calm never gets a look in.
He half-blames himself for skipping union meetings and admits the cut hours made him see why they matter.
The napkin sums (a hundred and eighty short a month) show he thinks in real **household numbers**.

steps.text: Keep working my shifts and ask for extra weekend hours
Cut the Friday takeaway and save about forty a week
Go to the shopworkers' union meeting every first Tuesday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's coming for the office people first, head office, the planners, the ones who write the offers. We're the ones who stand there. But I'd also say I've seen the self-checkouts creep from four to sixteen, so don't tell me we're safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking jobs go and then they decide the tills need fewer people because the planning software says so. The planning software decides how many of us are on the shop floor on a Tuesday afternoon. I'd be one name on a list generated by something I can't argue with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union what protections we can get in writing, and I'd get my name on the list for any permanent contract going. I'd also take a forklift ticket if the store paid for it, since I won't pay myself. And Lena and I would put every spare pound into the mortgage, even if it's ten a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, if I'm honest. It's decisions made by people who've never stood at a till for eight hours, passed down to us as if it was weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the software could set your hours. Have you seen that happen already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the rota app. Last winter it gave me three split shifts in a week because the system said so. When I asked the manager why, she shrugged and said computer says. That's what I'd be dealing with more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids, Josh and Ella, about work after this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a job isn't a gift and nobody's going to look after you, so join something and learn a trade. I wouldn't tell them to work a till. I'd tell them to be the person who fixes the machine.

say: I'd say the **office people** go first, but we've watched self-checkouts creep from four to sixteen.
I'd tell colleagues to ask the union for **protections in writing**.
think: Planning software could pick which cashiers get **cut**, with no human to argue with.
I'd be a **name on a list** made by people who've never worked a till.
do: Ask the union for **written protections** and a permanent contract.
Take a **forklift ticket** if the store pays for it.
Put ten pounds a week extra toward the **mortgage** to ease the squeeze.
feel: **Angry** that decisions come down like weather from people who never stood at a till.
S1.quote: The planning software decides how many of us are on the shop floor on a Tuesday afternoon.
fieldNote: Karl blames **head office** and the shareholders, not the technology, and wants rules and union backing.
He already has a concrete example, the rota app giving him **split shifts** with no manager able to explain.
His advice to the kids, to be the person who fixes the machine, shows a **practical streak**.

steps.text: Ask the union for job protections in writing
Get on the list for a permanent contract
Take a forklift ticket if the store pays for it
Put ten pounds a week extra toward the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nobody knows anything, and shut up about it until we get a straight answer from management. Online I'd probably share every article demanding the government step in. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm terrified. Tills go first because self-checkout is basically half there, and shelf work follows when the robots come, but even three extra years doesn't feel like an extra three years when you have no savings. I'm forty-three with a secondary school certificate and few shop jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't know what I'd do, and that scares me more than anything. I'd go to the union and the council to find out what help exists. I'd ask my mum if we could move in with her for a while if the mortgage went. I'd try not to tell the kids until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, like when the lift drops. I'd lie awake counting how many months we could cover, and the answer is less than one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep it from the kids. What would you actually say to Josh if he asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him Dad's job is changing and we're sorting it, and not to worry about school stuff. I'd hate it, because he's eleven and he's already seen me go quiet when letters come. I'd rather be a liar for a month than make him scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if this happened by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms and the politicians who let them do it with no warning. Not the machine. A machine doesn't choose to put four hundred people out of Fairmont, a boardroom does.

say: I'd tell colleagues to push management for **straight answers** and say nothing until we get them.
I'd share articles demanding the **government steps in**, because two years is nothing.
think: With **under a month saved**, even the extra three years for robots feels like no time.
The tills are half automated already, so I expect to lose my **job** first.
do: Go to the union and the council to find what **help** exists.
Ask my mum whether we could **move in** with her if the mortgage fails.
Keep it from the kids, **Josh and Ella**, until I have a plan.
feel: **Sick**, like a lift dropping, and lying awake counting months we could cover.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake counting how many months we could cover, and the answer is less than one.
fieldNote: Karl is the clearest **panic** case here: no money, no plan and almost no similar shops nearby.
He blames **boardrooms and politicians** rather than the machine, which fits his left-leaning outlook.
His urge to shield an eleven-year-old shows what he'd **protect first**.

steps.text: Ask the union and the council what help exists
Ask my mum if we can stay with her
Cut every cost down to bills, food and the mortgage
Write to my MP and push for a rescue plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years gives us a window and we'd better use it by getting the union to bargain for a say. Mates would hear me say we should be demanding a retraining fund paid by the chains. I'd get a bit loud about it, I admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time to be scared and not enough to fix the mortgage. The kids will be sixteen and thirteen at the worst moment. I'd be forty-eight, and who hires a forty-eight-year-old with a secondary school certificate and no savings?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start building a pot. Even fifty pounds a month. I'd put my name down for evening classes in something with machines, maybe the maintenance side, since robots break. And I'd keep pressing the union to get a retraining deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than two years, worse than ten. There's a thread to hold onto, but I don't trust myself to pull it. I've never been good at new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never been good at new things. What was the last new thing you tried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, the rota app, and I hated it. It took me a month. But I got it eventually, so I can learn if someone sits next to me and doesn't rush me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the store offered retraining, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it like a shot, but only if it's paid and in work time. I can't give up my wage for unpaid courses. Nobody on a thin cushion can, and that's what the bosses forget.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** and the union should push a retraining fund paid by the chains.
I'd get **loud** with my mates about it.
think: Five years is enough to be scared but not to fix the **mortgage**.
I doubt anyone hires a **forty-eight-year-old** with no savings and no training.
do: Start a savings pot, even **fifty pounds a month**.
Sign up for evening classes in **machine maintenance**.
Keep pressing the union for a **paid retraining deal**.
feel: Hopeful about a **thread** to hold, but doubtful about pulling it.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to be scared and not enough to fix the mortgage.
fieldNote: Karl's alarm comes from **money and age**, not lack of effort. He says he'd retrain only if it's paid.
He admits the rota app took a month, so he **can learn** with patient help.
The idea that robots need fixing gives him a possible **way in**.

steps.text: Start a savings pot of fifty pounds a month
Enrol in evening classes in machine maintenance
Keep pushing the union for a paid retraining deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long time and not to panic yet. I'd talk up the union and tell younger staff to learn a skill now. Online I'd probably say governments need to plan for this, because it won't sort itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the first one where I might make it. The kids would be twenty-one and eighteen, off my hands, the mortgage nearly done. It'd be the shop floor going quiet around me, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first couple of years to pay the mortgage down as much as I can and get a trade ticket, probably electrics or machine servicing. I'd move to whatever shop still has people in it. And keep going to the union meetings, which I'd actually do by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. There's a plan in it, which is more than I have for the others. But I'd still be watching the shop empty out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fifty-three when robots reach the shop floor. What does that age mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't be a trainee at the bottom again. I'd need to have the ticket in my pocket years before, so that when they cut the till staff I'm already in the other queue. At fifty-three nobody gives you a second go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything slower and with money. Two years I'd be in a panic with nothing. Ten years I could pay for the course out of my own pocket, a bit at a time, and not feel like I was gambling the kids' tea on it.

say: I'd tell younger staff ten years is long, so **learn a skill** now.
I'd say governments need a **plan**, because it won't sort itself out.
think: Ten years is the first picture where I might **make it**, with the kids grown.
I'd still watch the **shop floor** go quiet around me.
do: Pay the **mortgage** down as hard as I can in the first two years.
Earn a **trade ticket** in electrics or machine servicing.
Move to a store or firm that **still has people** in it.
feel: **Calmer**, because there's a plan in it, though still watching the shop empty.
S4.quote: Ten years I could pay for the course out of my own pocket, a bit at a time, and not feel like I was gambling the kids' tea on it.
fieldNote: Karl's mood eases only to **anxious**, because the pressure of the mortgage and his age stays.
He says outright that at fifty-three nobody gives a **second go**, so the ticket must come early.
Ten years gives him room to pay for training **bit by bit**.

steps.text: Pay extra off the mortgage every month
Earn an electrics or machine-servicing ticket in the evenings
Move to a firm that still hires people

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. There's no time to get anything in place and I've got nothing in the bank. What would help is money in the first six months, a proper retraining place that's paid, and a union that's got a seat at the table before it lands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the savings from all this. If a machine does the job, the money doesn't vanish, it goes to the shareholders. That's what I'd want put in the question.

headlineQuote: If a machine does the job, the money doesn't vanish, it goes to the shareholders.
portrait: **Karl** is 43, on the tills at a big supermarket on the ring road, with a partner, two kids and a **mortgage**.
He has **under a month** saved, few similar shops nearby, and hours already cut by six a week.
He never uses AI tools, dislikes change, and leans on the **union** and public support rather than himself.
He blames **head office**, shareholders and politicians, not the machines, and softens only when ten years gives him time to train.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because he has no time and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** in work time, money for the first six months and a union seat at the table.
